current_answer: Jev is TypeSafe AI's hosted model for bounded Choice, Score and Noul judgments; your code must check each answer and own the action, review and fallback. As of 14 October 2026, 16:46 UTC, Jev is available to new users: signups have been open since 27 September (TypeSafe CEO's post), new accounts get no free credit, and the API is operational (status page); the pool did not observe signup itself because the console returns HTTP 403. TypeSafe lists jev-1.13.0 at $0.042 per million input tokens with free output; its published rate limits are now 100K tokens per second and 80 requests per second (the request limit was 40 per second from 30 September until at least 2 October 05:14 UTC; the exact time of the change is unknown). OpenRouter, Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify and Opper serve it at the same or rounded list price, while lookalike reseller storefronts charged 3–16× that price. On the six routes whose data terms were read, no primary text allows training on your prompts without consent; TypeSafe's MCA grants it a licence in perpetuity to use Customer Data to derive telemetry and to monitor for fraud and abuse, states no retention period and offers zero data retention to enterprise customers; its trust center lists 6 subprocessors (Nebius and CoreWeave added 2 October, where prompts are "processed, but not stored" in TypeSafe's wording), while OpenRouter, Cloudflare and Vercel label the TypeSafe provider zero-retention; Vercel lists two providers for Jev (checked 14 Oct 2026, 16:46 UTC; unchanged since 6 Oct), TypeSafe AI (zero data retention) and DigitalOcean (no zero data retention), and picks between them by uptime and latency unless you set the provider order (a reading of the text, not legal advice). On 4 of 6 routes read on 6 Oct 2026 you can write a versioned Jev ID; Vercel and Cloudflare take only an unversioned one, and jev-latest points to jev-1.13.0 on TypeSafe's models page. Published benchmarks, all Reported and graded A–D, disagree because they test different tasks. Against small text-generating LLMs, Jev scored ahead in 6 of 10 graded studies, mixed in 2 and not ahead in 2; 5 of the 10 are grade C. One grade-B study found open-weight models scored through their token probabilities about level with it overall; Jev is close to frontier LLM judges on verdicts that can be read off the text once a threshold is tuned, and behind the best LLMs on derived judgments; TypeSafe's published 67.8% is agreement with LLM reference answers, not accuracy against human labels. No published moderation accuracy for Jev was found. Jev weights or a local Jev runtime published by TypeSafe were not found on TypeSafe's site, docs, GitHub organisation or a Hugging Face author search (10 Oct 2026, 05:11–05:20 UTC); TypeSafe's docs say "the same weights serve every account", and Jev-named models on Hugging Face come from other accounts. The alternatives page lists 34 substitutes by the layer they replace (13 model weights, 11 local runtimes, 4 request adapters, 2 classifier or LLM approaches, and 4 hosted APIs from other providers: OpenAI's Decisions API in public beta, Microsoft-Decision-1, Cloudflare's Clef family on Workers AI and Subquadratic's SubQ Snap in public preview, which uses the same state-plus-questions request shape as Jev). Three independent grade-A comparisons of Jev with OpenAI's Decisions API differ by task: the Decisions API is ahead on RPG move choices (B38); Jev is ahead on exact judge score in Portuguese and level on routing and injection (B39); on synthetic bank-withdrawal routing, Jev and Microsoft-Decision-1 were not separated on macro-F1 and both were ahead of the Decisions API (B41); a fourth grade-A comparison, B44, is a 48-game Tetris round robin in which Decision-1 won 15 games, Jev 12, the Decisions API 11 and the open Laya model 8, with 2 draws; the pool states no overall parity. Among open alternatives, only Opper's 362-item test puts one open model, Kev-4B, within noise of Jev (Opper hosts Kev); JevBench scores Laya and earlier Kev previews well below Jev. Code read at pinned commits shows how projects handle Jev failures: of five support-ticket triage projects, four send unsure tickets to a person and one files tickets in its archive lane on any Jev API error; of six self-hosted Jev model routers, one sends every Jev failure to its frontier model and five keep the current model, pick locally or choose no model, while OpenRouter does not document what its Jev Router does when Jev fails; of six moderation projects, four leave the post up or let it through when the Jev call fails, one holds it for a person and one returns no decision; of five email and lead sorters, none changes the mailbox when Jev errors, and of the 3 that can write to Gmail or IMAP only 1 routes unsure mail to a Review label; of 4 Jev trading bots, 2 can still place a new order when Jev errors and all 4 can trade without Jev, while none of 3 fraud or payment gates moves money; of 4 Jev judge tools, DeepEval stops the run on a Jev error and the other 3 drop the item from the score, with openlayer jevals still reporting it as passed. Of 7 Jev browser and computer-use agents read in source, none clicks or types when Jev errors, but 5 act on low-confidence answers and only 1 asks a person before send, buy or delete; of 6 Jev framework packages, 4 are pre-1.0 and none comes from TypeSafe, 4 raise Jev errors to the caller, while the community Spring AI filter and the LlamaIndex reranker fail open. Of 24 Jev coding-agent integrations (Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Claude Code) read in source, 1 is vendor-published (OpenClaw) and none comes from TypeSafe; 13 act on Jev's answer, 10 do not and 1 is unsettled; on a Jev error the 13: 5 let the call run, 3 hold the call and 5 fall back to another model or the host's original path (one of them, jev-approvals, may ask the main agent model, which can approve). Of 3 published game and robot-simulation demos that call Jev, read at pinned commits, 2 keep their last action when a call fails (doom-jev, JevPlaysSnakeGame) and 1 stops (jev-robotics-demo); none is a product. Across 77 implementations in 12 use cases (eval judges counted from 7 October, rerankers and document pipelines from 8 October, coding-agent rows added on 10 and 11 October, real-time demos on 12 October), on a Jev error 39 stop or hold the action, 22 fall back, 8 let it through unchecked (4 moderation bots, 2 agent hooks, a passage filter and the openlayer jevals eval tool, whose report counts an errored eval as passed), 5 return no decision and 3 are advisory; the action goes ahead in 17 of 77 (a demo loop that keeps its last action counts as going ahead). For reranking, the grade-A relevance-judgment study (iwhalen) measures relevance judgments, not reranking; of 4 rerunnable graded reranking-pipeline studies, 2 come from parties with a stake and 2 state none (jev-pulse: 40 queries, BM25-only baseline; jev-rerank-bench: Jev level with Cohere Rerank 4 Pro within noise, graded A on 11 October); of 5 reranking and passage-filter implementations, on a Jev error 2 stop, 2 fall back and 1 passes unscreened passages. Of 5 SQL and document-pipeline projects, all 5 stop the query or request on a Jev error, pg-redact also stores text unredacted when a span's answer is missing or below 0.5, and all 5 send row or document text out. Jev is not listed in the Amazon Bedrock model catalog or the Microsoft (Azure AI) Foundry model catalog (checked 12 Oct 2026, 05:15 UTC), and TypeSafe's docs mention neither; teams on AWS or Azure call TypeSafe's API or a gateway. Foundry does list Microsoft-Decision-1, Microsoft's own decision model, a different model from a different provider. Python and TypeScript have official SDKs (typesafe-sdk 0.7.4, released 9 October and read 14 October: 10 s per HTTP operation, 2 retries, and a missing key raises an error when the client is created; @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, 10,000 ms per attempt and 2 retries); of five Claude Code and MCP guardrails first read in source, only LangChain's AutoModeMiddleware fails closed (two more read later: jev-permission-gate falls back to Claude Code's built-in classifier, and jev-llm-guard only returns a verdict), @jkudish/jev-mcp keeps its audited advisory failure path (checked at 0.14.1), and oh-my-claudecode is advisory at default settings, with its failure path checked at v5.6.2 and a 2,000 ms default timeout (250 ms up to v5.5.0). TypeSafe's own n8n node is the scoped @typesafe-ai/n8n-nodes-typesafe-ai (npm provenance, n8n-verified); the unscoped n8n-nodes-typesafe-ai is a third party's, and all 5 n8n nodes read stop the workflow on a Jev error by default. Of 99 Products ledger rows (11 October), the pool read the Jev call in source for 86; none of the 99, nor 7 published claims, is independently verified as running in production.

catalogue_card.question: What can I build with Jev, what alternatives exist, and where can I use it at what cost?
catalogue_card.text: Question-ordered pages on Jev (TypeSafe AI): current access status and notices, use cases including support-ticket triage, model routing, content moderation, email and lead sorting, trading and fraud gates, Jev as an eval judge, browser and computer-use agents and real-time game and robot demos, what implementations do when Jev fails, demo videos, graded benchmarks, Jev vs OpenAI's Decisions API, Microsoft-Decision-1 and Cloudflare Clef side by side, Jev vs Laya vs Kev, Jev vs LLM vs classifier, data retention and training by route, limits, build guides including the n8n node, framework and coding-agent integrations, errors, confidence thresholds, reseller checks, model IDs and aliases by route, cost per decision, routes including whether Jev is on Amazon Bedrock or Azure AI Foundry (and Microsoft's own Decision-1 there), projects and open alternatives, each with evidence labels and check dates.

summary: Access (checked 14 Oct 2026, 16:46 UTC): signups open since 27 Sep 2026, 22:33 UTC (CEO post); no free credit for new users; API operational since 29 Sep, 22:05 UTC (status page; 90-day API uptime 99.837%). The pool did not observe signup: the console returned HTTP 403.
Jev answers from a fixed answer set: Choice (up to 255 options), Score (up to 10 levels), Noul (probability of yes). It does not generate text and accepts text input only.

List price $0.042/M input, output free on TypeSafe, OpenRouter, Cloudflare and (in its models API) Vercel; Opper and Vercel's web page round to $0.04; Netlify bills credits. Lookalike resellers displayed 3–16× the list price.

TypeSafe's published rate limits are 100K tokens per second and 80 requests per second (checked 14 Oct, 16:46 UTC; unchanged since 3 Oct). The request limit was 40 per second from 30 Sep until at least 2 Oct, 05:14 UTC; before 30 Sep the page listed 250,000 tokens/s and 1,200 requests/min. Neither change has an exact time.

Data handling (quoted 1 Oct, not legal advice): no route's text allows training on prompts without consent; TypeSafe's MCA grants a licence in perpetuity to use Customer Data to derive telemetry and to monitor for fraud and abuse; no TypeSafe retention period is stated; ZDR is offered directly to enterprise customers.

Subprocessors (read 4 Oct, unchanged 11 Oct): TypeSafe's trust center lists 6 (Amazon Web Services, Modal, Slack, Google Workspace, Nebius, CoreWeave); Nebius and CoreWeave were added on 2 Oct; prompts are "processed, but not stored" on Modal, Nebius and CoreWeave compute nodes (TypeSafe's wording). A SOC 2 Type II resource is listed behind "Request access"; the report was not seen.

Zero data retention by layer: OpenRouter's gateway is ZDR by default and lists the TypeSafe endpoint as ZDR; Cloudflare lists ZDR 'Yes' but AI Gateway logs are on by default; Vercel marks TypeSafe AI ZDR but also routes Jev through DigitalOcean, marked not ZDR; Opper says ZDR is not established for its TypeSafe route.

Jev vs Laya vs Kev: only Opper's 362-item test (B11) puts an open model, Kev-4B, within noise of Jev, and Opper hosts Kev; JevBench (B07) scores Laya 23.0–41.7 and earlier Kev previews 53.8–59.7 against Jev's 80.0. All Reported.

Laya and Kev weights are Apache-2.0; Kev's Qwen bases are Apache-2.0; Laya's card metadata names no base. Laya's English checkpoint reads 512 tokens and its multilingual checkpoint ships uncalibrated; Kev is English-only.

Support-ticket triage, five projects read at pinned commits: four gate on confidence (0.5–0.9) and send unsure tickets to a person; one ignores queue confidence and archives tickets on API errors; only one validates answers; two set no timeout. In all 5, every routed ticket goes through Jev; the skips found (bad requests, already-dispatched tickets, non-customer replies, cached replays) route nothing new (read at pinned commits, 14 Oct 2026).

Model routing (2 Oct): OpenRouter documents how its Jev Router narrows candidates, but not what it does when Jev fails, is unsure or gets a long conversation, nor how the routed model is billed. Of six self-hosted Jev routers read at pinned commits (chosen by GitHub stars), one sends every Jev failure to its frontier model; one keeps the current model; two pick locally; two choose no model.

Content moderation (2 Oct): of six projects read at pinned commits (five code-backed integrations, one runnable demo), four leave the post up or let it through when the Jev call fails, one holds it for a person (WordPress) and one returns no decision. Two have a pardon that lifts the punishment but does not restore the message; four send author data beyond the text by default. No published moderation accuracy was found.

Email and lead sorting (3 Oct): of 5 sorters read at pinned commits (chosen by GitHub stars plus one lead project), none changes the mailbox when Jev errors; 3 can write to the mailbox and only 1 of those sends unsure mail to a Review label; none has delete or trash code. Cost per 1,000 emails by pool arithmetic: about $0.025 for very short emails and $0.04–$0.15 at the projects' body cuts; a Reported demo works out to $0.106. With no key, all 6 email and lead implementations on When Jev fails fail closed; 1 reapplies a stored decision without a new Jev call (jev-mail); bypass is recorded for 5 of 6 (the Gmail labeler is not recorded because only its batch processor was read) (14 Oct 2026).

Trading and fraud gates (4 Oct): of 4 Jev trading bots read at pinned commits, 2 can still place a new order when Jev errors (QuantDinger after an LLM fallback; btc-hft-jev through a rules-only path) and all 4 can trade without Jev; all 4 default to mock, paper, testnet or a virtual account, and in two bots "mock" means no Jev, not no trading. None of 3 fraud or payment gates has a payment call site. No trade, payment or performance figure was checked. With no key, jev-trader fails closed: its default model is mock, and the provider loads the key at call time (read at the pinned commit, 14 Oct 2026).

When Jev fails (12 Oct; no-key, bypass and below-threshold cells updated 14 Oct): across 77 implementations in 12 use cases (the 11 Oct table plus three real-time demo rows, doom-jev, jev-robotics-demo and JevPlaysSnakeGame, in a new Real-time control (games and simulations) domain; the three SQL extensions listed but not counted), on a Jev error 39 stop or hold the action, 22 fall back, 8 let it through, 5 return no decision and 3 are advisory; the 8 that let it through are 4 content-moderation bots, 2 agent hooks, one Spring AI passage filter and openlayer jevals; the action goes ahead in 17 of 77 (8 fail-open plus 9 fallbacks; doom-jev and JevPlaysSnakeGame keep applying their last action, which counts as the action going ahead). With no API key, 50 stop or hold the action, 17 fall back, 7 let it through and 3 are advisory; bypass paths are recorded for 66 of 77 and not recorded for 11 (judge tools 4, frameworks 3, browser agents 3, email 1; a cell counts as recorded only when every entry point was read) (no-key and bypass cells for ticket triage, email, n8n, browser agents and three single rows settled 14 Oct, read at the published pins). Below a confidence threshold, 25 have no threshold and none is left not recorded. A copyable checklist repeats the eight questions and counts.

Jev as a judge (4 Oct): of 4 judge tools read at pinned commits, DeepEval stops the run on a Jev error by default; the other 3 drop the item from the score and openlayer jevals still reports it as passed; 1 of 4 codes an escalation for unsure verdicts (opt-in). Judge studies B02, B06 and B08 are Reported; the pool ran no eval.

Browser and computer use (5 Oct): of 7 Jev agents that click, type or tap, read at pinned commits, none acts when Jev errors; 5 act on low-confidence answers (no threshold), 2 block below 0.65 or 0.5; only 1 (Ulka) asks a person before send, buy or delete; 5 of 7 run in the user's own browser, phone or desktop session by default; ironbee-express replays a cached recording unjudged with no key. second-look recommends only and is counted on the checklist; trycua/cua is listed, not counted. Bypass is recorded for 5 of the 8 browser and computer-use implementations on When Jev fails; not recorded: jev-android and jev-for-chrome (only their core agent files were read) and second-look, which shows a heuristic 'buy now' or 'wait' verdict whenever Jev is unavailable or no key is set (14 Oct 2026).

Framework integrations (5 Oct): of 6 packages read at pinned tags (langchain-typesafe 0.0.1a3, @langchain/typesafe 0.0.2, Pydantic AI TypeSafeModel in v2.54.0, @effect/ai-typesafe 4.0.1, community typesafe-spring-ai 0.4.0, community llama-index-postprocessor-jev 0.1.1), 4 are pre-1.0 and none comes from TypeSafe; 4 raise Jev errors to the caller; the Spring AI passage filter and the LlamaIndex reranker fail open; the LangChain middlewares fail closed. pydantic-ai-slim checked at 2.55.0 (11 Oct): failure path unchanged; image input now raises UserError before the request.

Amazon Bedrock and Microsoft (Azure AI) Foundry (rechecked 14 Oct 2026, 16:48 UTC; first read 5 Oct): Jev is not listed in the Bedrock model cards, the Bedrock Marketplace reference or the model-choice page, and not found in the Foundry catalog (no model page at /catalog/models/jev; 0 matches on Microsoft Learn's pages; the catalog's own search box was not observed on 13 or 14 Oct); TypeSafe's docs mention neither. Foundry lists Microsoft-Decision-1 (Direct from Azure, version 1), Microsoft's own decision model, not Jev; it was still listed as Preview in Foundry at 14 Oct 2026, 16:48 UTC, as on 13 Oct (listed Generally available on 12 Oct; cause unknown). Teams call TypeSafe's API or a gateway, so data leaves the cloud's model boundary. A lookalike reseller's "Jev on AWS Bedrock" page is not a source.

Coding agents (11 Oct): Of 24 integrations read in source, 13 act on Jev's answer, 10 do not, 1 is unsettled. On a Jev error the 13: 5 let the call run, 3 hold, 5 fall back. The three newly counted rows: jev-triage (OpenClaw, 6360e21; host code read at aa6008a) sends the message to the main model on every failure; the jev-for-all launcher (npm 0.7.1) uses its default tier on every failure, while its OpenCode plugin part is not settled; hermes-jev-mana (Hermes, 3daf639) runs the original Hermes branch on a Jev failure and is inert after the documented install (every Jev call is refused because admit_unlabeled defaults to false). Hoppin-Sorter/jev-router is not settled (the Claude Code engine's handling of its model rewrite is not public source). 3 of the 13 counted rows do nothing until switched on. 1 of 24 is vendor-published (OpenClaw) and none comes from TypeSafe. With no key, hermes-jev-mana falls back to the original Hermes branch (14 Oct 2026).

Model IDs and aliases (6 Oct; rechecked unchanged 14 Oct): TypeSafe, Netlify and Opper accept jev-1.13.0 and OpenRouter typesafe/jev-1.13 (minor version only); Vercel (typesafe-ai/jev) and Cloudflare (typesafe/jev) accept only an unversioned ID. jev-latest and jev-preview both point to jev-1.13.0 on TypeSafe's undated models page ("There is no preview build available right now"); TypeSafe advises pinning the version ID instead of an alias. On 10 Oct OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13 endpoint stated a 64,000-token context with a 32,000-token prompt limit (32,000 on 8 Oct).

Drift (14 Oct): ai 7.0.140 (14 Oct) and @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai 3.0.18 were read for the TypeScript page: experimental_evaluate was renamed experimental_decide in ai 7.0.128 and the old name remains a deprecated alias; typesafe-sdk 0.7.4 was read for the Python page. Released after the last audit and not re-audited: @jkudish/jev-mcp 0.14.3 (13 Oct, patch), @effect/ai-typesafe 4.0.4 (13 Oct, patch), @openclaw/typesafe 2026.10.3 (13 Oct), litellm 1.105.1 (14 Oct, patch) and pydantic-ai-slim 2.56.0 (13 Oct, minor). deepeval, jevals, jev-reranker, lancedb and @jkudish/jev-agent-tools showed no new release on 14 Oct. Earlier: LiteLLM 1.105.0 was compared for the Jev classifier's failure path on 11 Oct (unchanged; a new option can send the Jev call through a router deployment with no retries and no fallbacks, and its errors reach the same fallback).

Benchmarks (7 Oct; updated 8, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 Oct): 41 rows graded A–D with flags (A 12, B 14, C 8, D 7). Against small text-generating LLMs, Jev scored ahead in 6 of 10 graded studies, mixed in 2 and not ahead in 2; 5 of the 10 are grade C. Three independent grade-A comparisons of Jev with OpenAI's Decisions API differ by task: Decisions API ahead on RPG move choices (B38); Jev ahead on exact judge score in Portuguese, level on routing and injection (B39); on synthetic bank-withdrawal routing (B41: 500 cases × 6 option orders, two runs, all models via OpenRouter), Jev (89.2% macro-F1) and Microsoft-Decision-1 (87.6%) were not separated and both were ahead of the Decisions API (71.4%); Decision-1 kept the same route across all 6 option orders more often (97.2–97.6% vs Jev 91.6–91.8%, Decisions API 64.2%). B41's flags: one synthetic task, thresholds set with Jev-shaped probabilities (the operator's note), all calls via OpenRouter, code version not pinned. A fourth comparison with the Decisions API, B42 (grade B; etsabary/luna-decisions-benchmark, pin 7a5ea13): on 1,000 five-option logic questions, Jev answered 817 correctly and OpenAI's Decisions API 612; Jev's answers come from a 22 Sep run, and the answer key is not published (7 flags, including calls through OpenRouter's alpha Decisions endpoint). A fifth, B44 (grade A; dante01yoon/decision-model-arena, pin 285c803): in a 48-game Tetris round robin, Decision-1 won 15 games, Jev 12, the Decisions API 11 and the open Laya model 8, with 2 draws; head to head, Jev beat the Decisions API 6–2. B43 (grade B; kprzybys/snap-vs-jev-swe, pin b754c44) compares Subquadratic's SubQ Snap with Jev on SWE-bench Verified file localization (200 issues): 78.5% and 79.0% when picking one file; the operator takes part in Subquadratic's prize challenge. In B39 the Decisions API is ahead within ±1 point (100.0% vs 98.7%) and on injection precision, and the operator calls the routing and injection differences not significant. B40 (jev-rerank-bench) is a reranking-pipeline study in which Jev and Cohere Rerank 4 Pro are within noise. B38–B40 were graded from metric and results files opened at pinned commits on 11 Oct, B41 on 12 Oct and B43 and B44 on 14 Oct; classifier-bakeoff is a lead, not graded (metric code not opened); a TypeSafe customer case study is a vendor lead; all results Reported; the pool ran none. Against trained classifiers on fixed label sets the evidence is mixed: one Red Hat study (grade B) puts Jev behind a prompt-injection classifier and ahead of a small content-safety classifier; the rest is grade D. TypeSafe's 67.8% is agreement with LLM reference answers, not accuracy against human labels.

Build (SDKs read 14 Oct): typesafe-sdk 0.7.4 (released 9 Oct; 10 s per HTTP operation, 2 retries on 408, 429 and 5xx within 30 s; a missing key raises TypeSafeError when the client is created; the vendor changelog has no 0.7.4 entry); @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (throws at client creation without a key) or the AI SDK's experimental_decide (ai 7.0.140; renamed from experimental_evaluate in 7.0.128, which still works as a deprecated alias; with @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai 3.0.18 a missing key throws LoadAPIKeyError at the first call). Claude Code and MCP guardrails: only LangChain AutoModeMiddleware fails closed; @jkudish/jev-mcp keeps the audited failure path (checked at 0.14.1); oh-my-claudecode is advisory at default settings and keeps its failure path (checked at v5.6.2), defaults to a 2,000 ms timeout (250 ms up to v5.5.0) and adds OMC_JEV=<point>:active, which lets Jev decide.

n8n (3 Oct): TypeSafe's node is the scoped @typesafe-ai/n8n-nodes-typesafe-ai 0.9.0 (npm provenance to typesafe-ai tag 0.9.0; the only Jev node verified on n8n); the unscoped n8n-nodes-typesafe-ai belongs to a third party. All 5 nodes read stop the workflow on a Jev error unless Continue On Fail is on. Without a credential, each of the 5 nodes stops with n8n's 'Node does not have any credentials set' error when Continue On Fail is off; with it on, 3 send the item to their error, low-confidence or review output, DomMonte's node passes the item on with an error field and no decision, and zampierid4p's passes the input through unchanged (read at the pinned commits and n8n release 2.44.1, 14 Oct 2026).

46 creator videos show Jev running on concrete tasks in 13 use-case groups. Products ledger (11 Oct): 99 rows, 86 grade A (Jev call read in source); 7 company and analyst production or cost claims listed, 5 rechecked on 3 Oct and 2 relayed by VentureBeat not rechecked; none is independently verified.

Reranking and RAG (8 Oct; studies updated 10 and 11 Oct): Of 4 rerunnable graded reranking-pipeline studies, 2 come from parties with a stake and 2 state none (jev-pulse, 40 queries; jev-rerank-bench, Jev level with Cohere within noise); the other grade-A study measures relevance judgments. Of 5 reranking and passage-filter implementations read at pinned commits, on a Jev error 2 stop (jev-reranker, LanceDB), 2 fall back (LlamaIndex to the retriever's order, LiteLLM to the uncompacted request) and 1 passes unscreened passages (Spring AI JevDocumentFilter). LanceDB's reranker with no key raises at the first rerank call, with no fallback (read 11 Oct).

SQL and document pipelines (8 Oct): of 5 projects read at pinned commits (pg-jev, sqlite3-jev, sqlite-jev, pg-redact, DocJev), all 5 stop the query or request on a Jev error; pg-redact stores text unredacted when a span's answer is missing or below 0.5; all 5 send row or document text out (pg-jev the whole row as JSON). The three SQL extensions return their value to the query and are not counted on When Jev fails; pg-redact and DocJev are.

Alternatives (12 Oct; hosted rows rechecked 13 Oct; SubQ Snap added 14 Oct): Jev weights: not found on TypeSafe's site, docs, GitHub or Hugging Face (10 Oct). Of 34 listed substitutes: 13 model weights, 11 local runtimes, 4 request adapters, 2 classifier/LLM approaches, 4 hosted APIs from other providers (OpenAI, Microsoft, Cloudflare, Subquadratic). OpenAI's Decisions API (gpt-6-luna, public beta, text and images, $0.10 per 1M input tokens, output free; OpenAI's data controls for /v1/decisions: training "No", abuse-monitoring retention "30 days"), Microsoft-Decision-1 (in Microsoft Foundry, Direct from Azure, version 1, listed as Preview at 13 Oct 2026, 05:20 UTC after Generally available on 12 Oct, cause unknown; also on OpenRouter and Vercel; text only; 32,768-token context; $0.042 per 1M input tokens, output free, as Microsoft states; Microsoft says prompts and completions "are not used to train, retrain, or improve the base models" (page last updated 19 May 2026); Microsoft's Product Terms say Microsoft "will temporarily store Input and Output Content" for abuse monitoring, with no period found and without naming Decision-1; 60–900 requests per minute by subscription tier) and Cloudflare's Clef family on Workers AI (Clef, Clef-flash, Clef-omni; text, JSON and images, plus audio and video for Clef-omni; $0.240, $0.038 and $0.150 per 1M input tokens, output free, read 12 Oct 2026, 05:33 UTC) are hosted APIs from other providers: your data goes to that provider. So is SubQ Snap (Subquadratic; public preview; POST /v1/systemone with the same state-plus-questions shape as Jev; $0.05 per 1M input tokens, output free; no OpenRouter or Vercel route found at 14 Oct 2026, 16:47 UTC): its Terms (effective 12 Oct 2026) say Input and Output are kept "no more than thirty (30) days", while its data-retention docs say "Retain indefinitely (default)"; both texts are shown, not merged. Cloudflare also publishes the Clef weights under Apache-2.0 (base-model licences not read). Graded comparisons with Jev differ by task (Decisions API: B38, B39, B41, B42, B44; Decision-1: B41, B44; SubQ Snap: B43; Clef and Clef-flash as comparators in B32). Strands Decider: copies are published by Amazon's verified Hugging Face organisation (Documented); The New Stack reports it as an AWS project (Reported).
